title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 865–867 (Night 202, continuing nights-201), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 202 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. When Marzawān points out the islands of King al-Ghayūr, the prince rejoices and embraces him; they enter the city, take lodging in a khan and rest three days from the journey. Then Marzawān takes Qamar al-Zamān to the bath, dresses him as a merchant, and has made for him a geomancer's sand-board of gold, a set of instruments and an astrolabe of silver plated with gold. He tells him to stand beneath the king's palace and cry out that he is the reckoner, the scribe, the sage and astrologer who knows the sought and the seeker; the king will send for him and bring him in to the Lady Budūr, his beloved. Once with her he is to ask for three days' grace, make himself known to her, and she will recover from her madness in a single night; her father will rejoice, marry him to her and share his kingdom with him. Qamar al-Zamān takes the gear and goes to the palace and proclaims himself in rhyming cries. The townspeople, who have seen no scribe or astrologer for a long while, crowd round, marvel at his beauty, and one of them begs him not to throw his life away for the princess, pointing to the heads hung up of all who tried before him. He pays no heed, telling himself that only one who suffers longing knows it, and goes on crying out, until morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and second night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the second after the two hundred”: al-thāniya, “the second”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا قَالَ لَهُ مَرْزَوَانُ انْظُرْ هٰذِهِ جَزَائِرُ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ فَرِحَ وَشَكَرَ عَلَي فِعْلِهِ وَقَبَّلَهُ وَضَمَّهُ إِلَى صَدْرِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā qāla lahu Marzawānu unẓur hādhihi jazāʾiru al-maliki al-Ghayūri fariḥa wa-shakara ʿalā fiʿlihi wa-qabbalahu wa-ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when said to-him Marzawān, “Look, these (are the) islands (of) the-king al-Ghayūr,” rejoiced, and-gave-thanks for his-deed, and-kissed-him and-pressed-him to his-breast.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Marzawān said to Qamar al-Zamān, “Look: these are the islands of King al-Ghayūr,” the prince rejoiced, thanked him for what he had done, kissed him and pressed him to his breast.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the end of the night before and tells it over in brief. The sentence is built as anna Qamara al-Zamāni … fariḥa: the subject is named first, in the accusative after anna, then the lammā clause is set inside, and the main verb fariḥa, “he rejoiced”, follows it. shakara ʿalā, “to thank for”: ʿalā marks what one is thanked for. The print spells it علي, with the two dots of yāʾ, where it usually writes على; it is the same word ʿalā and is kept as printed. ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi, “pressed him to his breast”: ilā marks where. The shaddas of قبّله and ضمّه and the ئ of جزائر are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَا إِلَى الْجَزَائِرِ دَخَلَا الْمَدِينَةَ وَأَنْزَلَهُ مَرْزَوَانُ فِي خَانٍ وَاسْتَرَاحَا ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ مِنَ السَّفَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalā ilā al-jazāʾiri dakhalā al-madīnata wa-anzalahu Marzawānu fī khānin wa-istarāḥā thalāthata ayyāmin mina al-safari
sentences.l: And-when they-two-arrived at the-islands, they-two-entered the-city, and-lodged-him Marzawān in a-khan, and-they-two-rested three days from the-journey.
sentences.i: When they reached the islands they entered the city, and Marzawān lodged him in a khan, and they rested there three days from their journey.
sentences.n: anzala, Form IV of nazala, “to make alight”, so “to put up, lodge” someone. A khān is an inn for travellers and merchants, built round a courtyard. thalāthata ayyāmin, “three days”, accusative of time; the print writes ثلثة without its alif, and the dagger alif supplies it. istarāḥa min, “to rest from”: min marks what one rests from.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَخَذَ مَرْزَوَانُ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَدَخَلَ بِهِ الْحَمَّامَ وَأَلْبَسَهُ لِبْسَ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika akhadha Marzawānu Qamara al-Zamāni wa-dakhala bihi al-ḥammāma wa-albasahu libsa al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And-after that, took Marzawān Qamar al-Zamān and-entered with-him the-bath, and-clothed-him (in the) dress (of) the-merchants.
sentences.i: After that Marzawān took Qamar al-Zamān to the bath and dressed him in the clothes of a merchant.
sentences.n: dakhala bihi al-ḥammāma, “he entered with him the bath”: dakhala bi-, “to go in with”, means “to take in, bring”; bi- marks the one taken along, and the place is the direct object. albasa, Form IV of labisa, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the garment: albasahu libsa al-tujjāri. libs, “dress, clothing”. The shadda of التجّار is printed.

sentences.t: وَعَمِلَ لَهُ تَخْتَ رَمْلٍ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ وَعَمِلَ لَهُ عُدَّةً وَعَمِلَ لَهُ أَسْطُرْلَابًا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ مَطْلِى بِالذَّهَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿamila lahu takhta ramlin min dhahabin wa-ʿamila lahu ʿuddatan wa-ʿamila lahu asṭurlāban min fiḍḍatin maṭlī bi-al-dhahabi
sentences.l: And-he-made for-him a-board (of) sand of gold, and-made for-him a-gear, and-made for-him an-astrolabe of silver, coated with-the-gold.
sentences.i: He had a geomancer's sand-board made for him of gold, and a set of instruments, and an astrolabe of silver plated with gold.
sentences.n: Marzawān fits the prince out as a travelling diviner. ʿamila lahu, “he made for him”: li- marks the one it is made for. takht raml, “a board of sand”, is the geomancer's tray: sand is strewn on it, figures are traced in it, and the future is read from them (ʿilm al-raml, “the science of sand”). min dhahabin, min fiḍḍatin: min marks the material, “of gold, of silver”. ʿudda, “equipment, gear”, the rest of the diviner's tools. asṭurlāb, “astrolabe”, a word from Greek, the astrologer's instrument for taking the height of the stars. maṭlī bi-al-dhahabi, “coated with gold”: bi- marks what it is coated with. maṭlī is the passive participle of ṭalā, “to smear, coat”; the print spells it مطلى, with ى and no ending, where Classical grammar would write مطليّا, maṭliyyan, agreeing with asṭurlāban. It is read here as the plain spoken form maṭlī. The shadda of عدّة is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ قُمْ يَا مَوْلَايَ وَقِفْ تَحْتَ قَصْرِ الْمَلِكِ وَنَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu qum yā mawlāya wa-qif taḥta qaṣri al-maliki wa-nādi
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Rise, O my-master, and-stand under (the) palace (of) the-king, and-call-out:
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Up, my lord: go and stand beneath the king's palace and cry aloud:
sentences.n: qum, “rise!”, imperative of qāma. qif, “stand!”, imperative of waqafa, which loses its first letter in the imperative; the print marks the kasra under its qāf. nādi, “call out!”, imperative of nādā, Form III: the final long vowel is cut short in the imperative, and the print marks the kasra that is left. yā mawlāya, “O my master”: Marzawān, though he is the guide, speaks to the prince as to his lord.

sentences.t: أَنَا الْحَاسِبُ أَنَا الْكَاتِبُ أَنَا الَّذِي أَعْرِفُ الْمَطْلُوبَ وَالطَّالِبَ أَنَا الْحَكِيمُ الْمَاهِرُ أَنَا الْمُنَجِّمُ الْبَاهِرُ فَأَيْنَ الطَّالِبُ
sentences.tr: anā al-ḥāsibu anā al-kātibu anā alladhī aʿrifu al-maṭlūba wa-al-ṭāliba anā al-ḥakīmu al-māhiru anā al-munajjimu al-bāhiru fa-ayna al-ṭālibu
sentences.l: I (am) the-reckoner, I (am) the-scribe, I (am) the-one-who knows the-sought and-the-seeker; I (am) the-sage the-skilful, I (am) the-astrologer the-dazzling; so-where (is) the-seeker?
sentences.i: ‘I am the reckoner, I am the scribe; I know the thing sought and the one who seeks it! I am the sage, the adept; I am the astrologer, the dazzling one! Where, then, is the one who seeks?’
sentences.n: The diviner's cry is in rhymed prose (sajʿ): al-ḥāsib / al-kātib / al-ṭālib, then al-māhir / al-bāhir, and the cry comes back to al-ṭālib at the end. Each phrase is a bare nominal sentence, anā al-…, “I (am) the …”. al-maṭlūb wa-al-ṭālib, “the thing sought and the seeker”: passive and active participle of ṭalaba, “to seek”, side by side. bāhir, “dazzling, surpassing”, from bahara, “to dazzle, outshine”.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ الْمَلِكَ إِذَا سَمِعَكَ يُرْسِلُ خَلْفَكَ وَيَدْخُلُ بِكَ عَلَى ابْنَتِهِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ مَحْبُوبَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-inna al-malika idhā samiʿaka yursilu khalfaka wa-yadkhulu bika ʿalā ibnatihi al-malikati Budūra maḥbūbatika
sentences.l: For the-king, when he-hears-you, sends behind-you and-goes-in with-you upon his-daughter the-princess Budūr, your-beloved.
sentences.i: For when the king hears you, he will send for you and bring you in to his daughter, the Princess Budūr, your beloved.
sentences.n: inna puts al-malika in the accusative; its predicate is yursilu, and the condition idhā samiʿaka, “when he hears you”, stands between. After idhā the perfect samiʿa looks to the future, and the result is a plain imperfect, “he sends”. arsala khalfa, “to send behind”, that is, “to send for, summon”. dakhala bi- … ʿalā, “to go in with someone to”: bi- marks the one brought, ʿalā the person visited, so “bring you in to”. Budūr is diptote, and in apposition takes -a in the genitive.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا دَخَلْتَ عَلَيْهَا قُلْ لَهُ أَعْطِنِي مُهْلَةً ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ فَإِنْ طَابَتْ زَوِّجْنِي بِهَا وَإِنْ لَمْ تَطِبِ افْعَلْ بِي كَمَا فَعَلْتَ بِالَّذِينَ قَبْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-idhā dakhalta ʿalayhā qul lahu aʿṭinī muhlatan thalāthata ayyāmin fa-in ṭābat zawwijnī bihā wa-in lam taṭibi ifʿal bī kamā faʿalta bi-alladhīna qablī
sentences.l: So-when you-enter upon-her, say to-him: Give-me a-respite (of) three days; so-if she-gets-well, marry-me with-her, and-if not she-gets-well, do with-me as you-did with-those-who (were) before-me.
sentences.i: When you go in to her, say to him: ‘Give me three days' grace: if she recovers, marry me to her, and if she does not, do with me as you did with those who came before me.’
sentences.n: qul lahu, “say to him”: to the king. After idhā the main clause qul comes without fa-, where Classical grammar would want fa-qul; the edition often drops it. muhla, “respite, delay”, and thalāthata ayyāmin, “three days”, gives its measure. ṭābat, of the sick, “she got well”; after in the perfect looks to the future. zawwaja bi-: the verb chooses bi- for the bride, “marry me to her”. lam taṭib, jussive after lam, the long vowel shortened. The answer ifʿal, “do!”, again stands without fa-. faʿala bi-, “to do to”: the verb chooses bi- for the one acted on, both in bī, “to me”, and in bi-alladhīna, “to those who”. qablī, “before me”: the suitors who came before and failed. The shadda of زوّجني is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ يَقْبَلُ مِنْكَ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu yaqbalu minka dhālika
sentences.l: For-indeed-he accepts from-you that.
sentences.i: He will grant you that.
sentences.n: qabila min, “to accept from”: min marks the one who makes the offer.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا صِرْتَ عِنْدَهَا عَرِّفْهَا بِنَفْسِكَ فَإِنَّهَا تَشْتَدُّ لَمَّا تَرَاكَ وَيَزُولُ مَا بِهَا مِنَ الْجُنُونِ وَهِيَ تَطِيبُ فِي لَيْلَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā ṣirta ʿindahā ʿarrifhā bi-nafsika fa-innahā tashtaddu lammā tarāka wa-yazūlu mā bihā mina al-junūni wa-hiya taṭību fī laylatin
sentences.l: So-when you-come-to-be with-her, make-known-to-her yourself; for-indeed-she grows-strong when she-sees-you, and-passes-away what (is) in-her of the-madness, and-she gets-well in a-night.
sentences.i: And once you are with her, make yourself known to her: when she sees you she will gather her strength, the madness that is on her will leave her, and she will be well in a single night.
sentences.n: ṣāra ʿinda, “to come to be with”. ʿarrafa … bi-, Form II, “to acquaint someone with”: bi- marks what is made known, here bi-nafsika, “with yourself”. ishtadda, Form VIII, “to grow strong”, of one recovering. lammā tarāka: lammā, “when”, here with the imperfect and a future sense, a later usage the Classical language does not have. mā bihā mina al-junūni, “what is in her of madness”: bi- of the place where the trouble lies, and min says what mā is. wa-hiya taṭību, “and she will be well”, with the subject put first. fī laylatin, “in one night”. The shaddas of عرّفها, فانّها and تشتدّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَأَطْعِمْهَا وَاسْقِهَا وَيَفْرَحُ أَبُوهَا بِسَلَامَتِهَا وَيُزَوِّجُكَ بِهَا وَيُقَاسِمُكَ فِي مُلْكِهِ لِأَنَّهُ شَرَطَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ هٰذَا الشَّرْطَ وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭʿimhā wa-isqihā wa-yafraḥu abūhā bi-salāmatihā wa-yuzawwijuka bihā wa-yuqāsimuka fī mulkihi li-annahu sharaṭa ʿalā nafsihi hādhā al-sharṭa wa-al-salāmu
sentences.l: So-feed-her and-give-her-drink; and-rejoices her-father at-her-safety, and-marries-you with-her, and-shares-with-you in his-kingdom, because-he stipulated upon himself this the-condition. And-the-peace.
sentences.i: Give her food and drink; then her father will rejoice at her recovery, marry you to her and share his kingdom with you, for he has bound himself by that condition. And that is all.”
sentences.n: aṭʿim, “feed!”, Form IV of ṭaʿima; isqi, “give to drink!”, from saqā, its final vowel shortened in the imperative. fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause; salāma, “safety, soundness”, is here her recovery. zawwaja bi- again, bi- for the bride. qāsama fī, Form III, “to share with someone in”: fī marks what is shared. sharaṭa ʿalā nafsihi, “he laid the condition on himself”: ʿalā marks the one bound by it, and the condition is the king's own promise about whoever should cure his daughter. wa-al-salāmu, “and peace”, closes a speech: “and that is all”. The shadda of ويزوّجك is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ قَالَ لَهُ لَا عَدِمْتُ فَضْلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni hādhā al-kalāma qāla lahu lā ʿadimtu faḍlaka
sentences.l: And-when heard Qamar al-Zamān this the-speech, he-said to-him: Not may-I-lack your-kindness!
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān heard this, he said to him, “May I never be without your kindness!”
sentences.n: lā ʿadimtu faḍlaka, “may I not lose your kindness”: lā with the perfect makes a wish, and this is a common formula of thanks. ʿadima, “to lose, be without”; faḍl, “bounty, kindness”.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ مِنْهُ الْعُدَّةَ وَخَرَجَ مِنَ الْخَانِ وَهُوَ لَابِسُ الْبَدْلَةِ وَأَخَذَ مَعَهُ الْعُدَّةَ الَّتِي ذَكَرْنَاهَا وَسَارَ إِلَى أَنْ وَقَفَ تَحْتَ قَصْرِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha minhu al-ʿuddata wa-kharaja mina al-khāni wa-huwa lābisu al-badlati wa-akhadha maʿahu al-ʿuddata allatī dhakarnāhā wa-sāra ilā an waqafa taḥta qaṣri al-maliki al-Ghayūri
sentences.l: And-he-took from-him the-gear, and-went-out from the-khan, and-he (was) wearing the-suit, and-took with-him the-gear which we-mentioned-it, and-went until that he-stood under (the) palace (of) the-king al-Ghayūr,
sentences.i: He took the instruments from him and went out of the khan, dressed in the merchant's suit, carrying the instruments we have spoken of, and walked on until he stood beneath the palace of King al-Ghayūr,
sentences.n: The sentence says twice that he took the gear, once from Marzawān and once with him; the storyteller is simply going over the ground again. wa-huwa lābisu al-badlati, “he wearing the suit”, a clause of state with wa-; lābis is the active participle of labisa, “to wear”. badla, “a suit of clothes”, a later word: the merchant's dress Marzawān had given him. allatī dhakarnāhā, “which we have mentioned”: the storyteller speaks in the first person plural, and -hā picks up allatī. ilā an, “until”. The first العدّة carries a printed shadda, the second does not.

sentences.t: وَنَادَى أَنَا الْكَاتِبُ الْحَاسِبُ أَنَا الَّذِي أَعْرِفُ الْمَطْلُوبَ وَالطَّالِبَ أَنَا الَّذِي أَفْتَحُ الْكِتَابَ وَأَحْسُبُ الْحِسَابَ وَأُفَسِّرُ الْأَحْلَامَ وَأَخُطُّ بِأَقْلَامِ الْمَطَالِبِ فَأَيْنَ الطَّالِبُ
sentences.tr: wa-nādā anā al-kātibu al-ḥāsibu anā alladhī aʿrifu al-maṭlūba wa-al-ṭāliba anā alladhī aftaḥu al-kitāba wa-aḥsubu al-ḥisāba wa-ufassiru al-aḥlāma wa-akhuṭṭu bi-aqlāmi al-maṭālibi fa-ayna al-ṭālibu
sentences.l: and-called-out: I (am) the-scribe the-reckoner, I (am) the-one-who knows the-sought and-the-seeker; I (am) the-one-who opens the-book and-reckons the-reckoning, and-interprets the-dreams and-traces with-(the)-pens (of) the-quests; so-where (is) the-seeker?
sentences.i: and cried aloud: “I am the scribe, the reckoner; I know the thing sought and the one who seeks it! I am he who opens the book and casts the count, who reads dreams and traces with the pens of every quest! Where, then, is the one who seeks?”
sentences.n: His cry is not quite the one Marzawān taught him, but it keeps the rhymed prose: al-ḥāsib / al-ṭālib, al-kitāb / al-ḥisāb, al-aḥlām on its own, then al-maṭālib / al-ṭālib. fataḥa al-kitāba, “to open the book”: diviners opened a book at random and read the answer from the page. ḥasaba al-ḥisāba, “to reckon the reckoning”, a verb with its own verbal noun as object, of the astrologer's calculations. fassara, Form II, “to interpret” dreams. khaṭṭa, “to draw lines”, is also the geomancer's word for tracing figures in the sand. bi-aqlāmi al-maṭālibi, “with the pens of the things sought”: bi- marks the tool. The phrase is loose: maṭālib, “things sought, wishes”, in the later language also meant hidden treasures, and a hint at treasure-finding cannot be ruled out, but the plain sense is “I write out the answer to every quest”. The shaddas of افسّر and اخطّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ أَهْلُ الْمَدِينَةِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ جَاؤُا إِلَيْهِ لِأَنَّ لَهُمْ مُدَّةً مَارَأَوْا كَاتِبًا وَلَا مُنَجِّمًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ahlu al-madīnati hādhā al-kalāma jāʾū ilayhi li-anna lahum muddatan mā raʾaw kātiban wa-lā munajjiman
sentences.l: And-when heard (the) people (of) the-city this the-speech, they-came to-him, because for-them (was) a-while (that) not they-saw a-scribe and-not an-astrologer.
sentences.i: When the people of the city heard this cry they came to him, for it was a long while since they had seen a scribe or an astrologer.
sentences.n: jāʾū, “they came”, is printed جاؤا, the hamza on a wāw that does duty for the long ū, where the full spelling is جاءوا; it is kept. ahl, “people”, is singular in form, but the verb is plural by sense. li-anna lahum muddatan mā raʾaw, “because they had a space of time (in which) they had not seen”: muddatan is the noun of anna, lahum its predicate set first, and mā raʾaw describes the time. The hanging heads in what follows tell why. The print sets mā raʾaw solid as مارأوا; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. Its hamza and the shadda of منجّما are printed.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفُوا حَوْلَهُ وَصَارُوا يَتَأَمَّلُونَهُ فَرَأَوْهُ عَلَى غَايَةٍ مِنَ الْجَمَالِ وَاللُّطْفِ وَالظَّرْفِ وَالْكَمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafū ḥawlahu wa-ṣārū yataʾammalūnahu fa-raʾawhu ʿalā ghāyatin mina al-jamāli wa-al-luṭfi wa-al-ẓarfi wa-al-kamāli
sentences.l: And-they-stood around-him, and-came-to be-gazing-at-him, and-they-saw-him at an-utmost of the-beauty and-the-charm and-the-grace and-the-perfection.
sentences.i: They stood about him and fell to gazing at him, and found him of the utmost beauty, charm, grace and perfection.
sentences.n: ṣārū yataʾammalūnahu, “they fell to gazing at him”: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin, set about”. taʾammala, Form V, “to look closely at”. raʾawhu ʿalā ghāyatin min, “they saw him at the utmost of”, the usual way of saying “supremely”. The list rhymes, al-jamāl / al-kamāl. The hamzas of يتأمّلونه and فرأوه and the shadda of يتأمّلونه are printed.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفُوا يَتَعَجَّبُونَ مِنْ حُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ وَقَدِّهِ وَاعْتِدَالِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafū yataʿajjabūna min ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi wa-qaddihi wa-iʿtidālihi
sentences.l: And-they-stood marvelling at his-beauty and-his-loveliness and-his-stature and-his-symmetry.
sentences.i: And they stood marvelling at his beauty and loveliness, his stature and his graceful proportion.
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to wonder at”: min marks what is wondered at. qadd, “stature”, and iʿtidāl, “evenness, good proportion”, are the stock pair for a handsome figure; jamālihi / iʿtidālihi rhyme. The shaddas of يتعجّبون and قدّه are printed.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ وَاحِدٌ وَقَالَ لَهُ بِاللّٰهِ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا الشَّابُّ الْمَلِيحُ صَاحِبَ اللِّسَانِ الْفَصِيحِ لَا تُخَاطِرْ بِنَفْسِكَ وَتَرْمِيَ رُوحَكَ فِى الْهَلَاكِ طَمَعًا فِي زَوَاجِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama ilayhi wāḥidun wa-qāla lahu bi-Allāhi ʿalayka ayyuhā al-shābbu al-malīḥu ṣāḥiba al-lisāni al-faṣīḥi lā tukhāṭir bi-nafsika wa-tarmiya rūḥaka fī al-halāki ṭamaʿan fī zawāji al-malikati Budūra binti al-maliki al-Ghayūri
sentences.l: And-came-forward to-him one, and-said to-him: By-God upon-you, O the-young-man the-comely, owner (of) the-tongue the-eloquent, do-not risk with-yourself and-throw your-soul into the-destruction, (in) desire for (the) marriage (of) the-princess Budūr, daughter (of) the-king al-Ghayūr;
sentences.i: Then one of them came up to him and said, “I adjure you by God, comely youth with the eloquent tongue, do not risk your life and cast yourself into destruction in hope of marrying the Princess Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr.
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God upon you”, an adjuration: bi- of the oath, and ʿalayka lays it on the one addressed. The address rhymes, al-malīḥ / al-faṣīḥ. ṣāḥiba al-lisāni, “owner of the tongue”, is read as a second vocative with yā unspoken, hence the accusative. khāṭara bi-, Form III, “to risk”: the verb takes bi- for what is staked. wa-tarmiya: after a prohibition, wa- with the subjunctive forbids the two things together, “do not risk yourself and so cast …”; the print's ترمي would also allow the Middle Arabic indicative tarmī. The print spells fī as فى, with ى; it is kept. ṭamaʿan fī, “out of desire for”, accusative of cause: fī marks what is coveted.

sentences.t: وَانْظُرْ بِعَيْنِكَ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الرُّؤُسِ الْمُعَلَّقَةِ فَإِنَّ أَصْحَابَهَا كُلَّهُمْ قُتِلُوا بِسَبَبِ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-unẓur bi-ʿaynika ilā hādhihi al-ruʾūsi al-muʿallaqati fa-inna aṣḥābahā kullahum qutilū bi-sababi dhālika
sentences.l: and-look with-your-eye at these the-heads the-hung-up, for their-owners, all-of-them, were-killed by-reason-of that.
sentences.i: Look with your own eyes at these heads hung up here: their owners were every one of them put to death for that very thing.”
sentences.n: ruʾūs, plural of raʾs, “head”, is printed الرؤس, with one wāw where the full spelling has two, الرؤوس; it is read ruʾūs. al-muʿallaqa, “hung up”, is feminine singular, agreeing with a plural of things. aṣḥābahā, “their owners”, the men whose heads they were. kullahum, “all of them”, follows in the same case to stress the whole. qutilū, passive, “they were killed”; the print marks its ḍamma. bi-sababi, “by reason of”. The shadda of المعلّقة is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ إِلَى كَلَامِهِ وَنَادَى بِأَعْلَى صَوْتِهِ أَنَا الْحَكِيمُ الْكَاتِبُ أَنَا الْمُنَجِّمُ الْحَاسِبُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yaltafit Qamaru al-Zamāni ilā kalāmihi wa-nādā bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi anā al-ḥakīmu al-kātibu anā al-munajjimu al-ḥāsibu
sentences.l: And-not turned Qamar al-Zamān to his-speech, and-called-out with-(the)-highest (of) his-voice: I (am) the-sage the-scribe, I (am) the-astrologer the-reckoner!
sentences.i: But Qamar al-Zamān paid no heed to his words, and cried out at the top of his voice, “I am the sage, the scribe! I am the astrologer, the reckoner!”
sentences.n: iltafata ilā, Form VIII, “to turn toward, pay heed to”: ilā marks what is heeded. bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi, “with the highest of his voice”, at the top of his voice: bi- marks the means. The cry rhymes, al-kātib / al-ḥāsib.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ كُلٌّ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبَلَدِ يَنْهَاهُ عَنْ هٰذَا الْفِعْلِ فَلَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ إِلَيْهِمْ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra kullun min ahli al-baladi yanhāhu ʿan hādhā al-fiʿli fa-lam yaltafit ilayhim abadan
sentences.l: And-came each-one of (the) people (of) the-town forbidding-him from this the-deed; and-not he-turned to-them ever.
sentences.i: Every one of the townsfolk tried to turn him from what he was doing, but he paid them no heed at all,
sentences.n: ṣāra kullun … yanhāhu, “each one set about forbidding him”: ṣāra with an imperfect again. kull with no genitive after it takes tanwīn, “each one”, and min ahli al-baladi says of whom. nahā ʿan, “to forbid from”: the verb chooses ʿan. lam … abadan, “not at all”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَا يَعْلَمُ الشَّوْقَ إِلَّا مَنْ يُكَابِدُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi mā yaʿlamu al-shawqa illā man yukābiduhu
sentences.l: And-he-said in himself: Not knows the-longing except who endures-it.
sentences.i: and said to himself, “None knows longing but the one who suffers it.”
sentences.n: A saying that echoes a well-known half-line of verse, lā yaʿrifu al-shawqa illā man yukābiduhu, “none knows longing but he who suffers it”; here it is set as prose, with mā yaʿlamu. mā … illā, “not … except”, that is “only”. kābada, Form III, “to struggle with, endure”. The shadda of الّا is printed.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ يُنَادِي بِأَعْلَى صَوْتِهِ أَنَا الْحَكِيمُ أَنَا الْمُنَجِّمُ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra yunādī bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi anā al-ḥakīmu anā al-munajjimu
sentences.l: And-he-came-to calling-out with-(the)-highest (of) his-voice: I (am) the-sage, I (am) the-astrologer!
sentences.i: And he went on crying at the top of his voice, “I am the sage! I am the astrologer!”
sentences.n: ṣāra yunādī, “he took to calling out”, ṣāra with the imperfect once more.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
